That pushed back the date at which extra Russian gas could reach a market already short of storage and losing the competition for LNG cargoes to Asia, so traders read continued Nord Stream 2 uncertainty as straightforwardly bullish.

annotations.what_happened: On Tuesday 5 October 2021 European gas contracts hit new records. Once the market accepted that Europe would exit winter comfortable, that premium came out of the far curve as well as the prompt, which is why the breach shows on Gas Sum-27 at -9.7% and the source explicitly notes the 2023/24 and 2024/25 winters softening alongside.

Probable rather than Confirmed for two reasons: it is a single source, and the driver it gives is genuinely a pair, mild weather and above-average inventories, rather than one named cause. The headline names mild weather because that is the proximate cause of both, the inventories being high because the

annotations.label: Colder late-February forecasts lift the gas complex
annotations.what_happened: European gas rose for a third straight session on Friday 24 February 2023, up 4% to above EUR52/MWh, as cooler temperatures forecast across northwest Europe for the following fortnight were expected to boost heating demand. The contract was on track for a weekly gain of almost 6%. Storage was about 63% full against a ten-year average of 54%, so the move was a demand-side revision rather than a supply scare. The UK benchmark did the same thing, recovering from a nine-month low of 119 pence a therm set on 21 February on the same cooler forecasts and on wind output dropping from 13.5 GW to 9.8 GW.
annotations.why_it_moved: Gas Sep-29 is six and a half years forward and has no weather content of its own, so the brief's rule applies: this is the curve moving with the market rather than the delivery month responding to news. What the market did that week was rally roughly 6% off a multi-year low on colder forecasts, and an illiquid far-dated point re-marked by more than the front did - 9.2% against the front's 6% - which is the normal behaviour of a thinly traded tail when the whole curve shifts.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary for both EU and UK benchmarks, dated inside the window. Probable, the ceiling the brief sets for that source. Deliberately not looking for a September 2029 story: per the brief, a far-dated month moving alone is curve repricing and the right thing to record is what the market did.

annotations.label: French strikes block LNG terminal imports
annotations.what_happened: Strikes against France's pension reform shut its LNG import/regasification terminals: deliveries from the four French terminals fell from ~1,165 GWh/d on 5 March to zero from 7 March, with at least seven LNG cargoes diverting to Britain, the Netherlands and Spain. European gas rose for a third straight day.
annotations.why_it_moved: France re-exports regasified LNG to the rest of Europe, so idling its terminals cut effective European supply and lifted gas and power forwards.

annotations.label: Warmer temperature forecasts denting demand
annotations.what_happened: British and Dutch wholesale gas prices fell on Thursday 16 March 2023 as forecasts for warmer temperatures dented demand. Uncertainty over French nuclear output and strikes at France's LNG terminals worked the other way and provided some support, limiting the fall rather than causing it. The move came in a week in which the European benchmark had already been making fresh multi-month lows on an unseasonably mild winter, record LNG arrivals and storage far above the five-year average.
annotations.why_it_moved: By mid-March the market was pricing the end of a winter Europe had comfortably survived. Warmer forecasts at that point do not just cut a few days of heating demand: they lock in a higher end-of-winter storage level, which cuts the volume that has to be bought back over the following injection season. That is why the selling ran down the curve, with Gas Sum-23 falling 20.0% on the week and eleven seasons breaching across both power and gas, rather than being confined to the prompt.

annotations.label: French strike extension and cold start to April
annotations.what_happened: In late March 2023 European power and gas edged higher as French pension strikes were extended (keeping LNG-terminal and refinery disruption in play) and forecasts pointed to a cold start to April; the TTF May contract recovered from EUR39.2/MWh on 20 March to EUR42.75 by 28 March.
annotations.why_it_moved: Continued French terminal disruption plus colder near-term weather tightened the prompt balance, lifting gas and power forwards off their mid-March lows.

annotations.label: Record LNG supply and weak demand sink gas to 2021 lows
annotations.what_happened: European gas fell below EUR40/MWh in the last week of April 2023, extending a 16% drop over the month and holding close to levels last seen in June 2021, on subdued demand and ample supply. Storage was building on record US LNG shipments and stood at 58% full across the EU, 65% in Germany and 87% in Spain; EU Energy Commissioner Kadri Simson said Europe was in good position to enter the next winter with confidence. German gas demand in March was 15% below the 2019-2021 average, with industrial use down 21%. EU carbon fell to EUR90 a tonne on 26 April, a three-month low, as weak industrial output cut permit demand and lower gas prices reduced gas-to-coal switching.
annotations.why_it_moved: This is the fuel-scope Both case working properly. Cheap, abundant gas pulls down the marginal cost of power generation directly, and the carbon price falling in the same week removes the other component of a gas plant's variable cost, so Electricity Jun-23 fell alongside Gas Jun-23 and Jul-23. The contracts that breached are the nearest summer delivery months, which are the ones most exposed to the fact that the storage refill Europe was worried about had already been achieved.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, both articles inside the window and the carbon piece dated on the label date itself. Probable, the source ceiling. Note this is the same week as ref 36 and the two rows point in opposite directions on different parts of the curve; the near-dated fall is well evidenced, which is part of why the far-dated rise in ref 36 reads as a re-mark rather than news.

annotations.label: Sixth straight weekly loss on weak power-sector demand
annotations.what_happened: On Friday 12 May 2023 European gas fell more than 6% to around EUR34/MWh, a sixth consecutive weekly loss and the longest losing run in over three years. Trading Economics reported that most European countries were seeing very low power demand and that gas burn for power generation had come in below expectations the previous month even against a sharp drop in coal burn. Strong LNG imports and high stockpiles after a mild winter had left European storage almost 60% full, well above the five-year average. The decline was continuous through the window: the contract had already fallen to EUR36 on 8 May, a level not seen since July 2021.
annotations.why_it_moved: Sep-23 and Oct-23 are the last injection month and the first winter month, the pair that price whether Europe will arrive at 1 November with enough gas. Storage running well above the five-year average in mid-May with two months of injection season still to go answered that question early, and gas-for-power demand failing to appear even as coal burn collapsed removed the one source of summer demand that could have absorbed the surplus. Both contracts had to give up the winter-adequacy premium they were still carrying.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated on the trigger day. Probable, the source ceiling.

annotations.label: European gas hits two-year low on ample LNG
annotations.what_happened: On Thursday 1 June 2023 European gas extended losses to below EUR24/MWh, a fresh two-year low, following a 30% drop through May. Trading Economics attributed the move to abundant LNG supplies, reduced consumption, mild weather, stronger renewable power generation and subdued Asian demand, with the European economy showing weakness - Germany in recession in the first quarter - and Chinese indicators pointing to a subdued recovery. The UK benchmark was below 56 pence a therm, the lowest since April 2021, with wind having overtaken gas as Britain's largest source of electricity in the first quarter of 2023 at 32.4% against 31.7%.
annotations.why_it_moved: Electricity Nov-23 is the first proper winter power month, priced off the expected cost of gas-fired generation in the peak demand period. Gas hitting a two-year low removed most of that cost base, and the specifically power-side component of the move - renewable generation displacing thermal plant, with UK wind output now exceeding gas over a full quarter - cuts the number of hours a gas plant is expected to set the price at all. Both effects push the same way on a winter power contract.

The fuel scope is Electricity-only against a driver that is largely a gas story, which the brief warns about; the mitigation here is that the same source names stronger renewable generation as one of the causes, and the UK commentary in the same window documents wind displacing gas in the generation mix, which is a genuinely p

annotations.label: Supply outages spark rebound from two-year low
annotations.what_happened: On Monday 5 June 2023 European gas traded above EUR26/MWh, rebounding from the two-year low below EUR23 set the previous week, on reduced supply. US LNG shipments were becoming scarcer as cargoes were funnelled to Asia, where summer cooling demand made prices more competitive; France's Montoir LNG terminal was closed for maintenance until 10 June; and the TurkStream pipeline carrying Russian gas through the Black Sea to Turkey was suspended until 12 June. Saudi Arabia's decision to make significant oil output cuts from July was also putting upward pressure on the oil-linked long-term contracts. Norway's Equinor had separately postponed the restart of its Hammerfest LNG plant.
annotations.why_it_moved: Gas Jul-23 was the front month, so it was the contract that had to clear against physical availability in a month when several sources of supply were simultaneously unavailable. A market that had fallen 66% year-to-date had no risk premium left in it, which is precisely why a cluster of ordinary outages could move the prompt 22% in a session: at EUR23/MWh there was nothing left to absorb a supply surprise.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated on the trigger day. Probable, the source ceiling. The commentary names several concurrent outages rather than one; recorded as a supply-outage cluster because no single one of them is large enough on its own and the source does not rank them.

annotations.label: Norwegian gas outages cut supply
annotations.what_happened: European gas jumped over 15% as Norwegian outages stacked up: on 13 June outages hit Ormen Lange, Nyhamna and Aasta Hansteen, and the Nyhamna restart was pushed to mid-July. TTF front-month rose to over EUR40/MWh by 15 June from ~EUR24 at the month's start.
annotations.why_it_moved: With Norway now Europe's top pipeline supplier, simultaneous unplanned outages sharply cut available supply, lifting gas and power forwards.

annotations.label: Extended Norwegian maintenance drives 50% rebound
annotations.what_happened: European gas rallied hard through the second week of June 2023, up more than 40% on the week to EUR33/MWh by 9 June and reaching a one-month high of about EUR36 on 13 June, before falling back 7% on 14 June when the market judged the move an overreaction. Trading Economics' 14 June retrospective is explicit about the cause: prices had jumped 50% from the two-year low below EUR23 in early June on supply concerns after extended maintenance work at Norwegian production facilities, with Equinor postponing the Hammerfest LNG restart to 14 June. Goldman Sachs was quoted putting the Norwegian tightening at 1.4 bcm against 3 bcm of loosening from weak demand and abundant LNG.
annotations.why_it_moved: Gas Jul-23 was the front month and Norway had by then replaced Russia as Europe's largest pipeline supplier, so extended outages there hit the prompt balance directly. As with the 5 June episode, the violence of the move reflects how little premium was in the price rather than the size of the outage: a 1.4 bcm supply loss produced a 21% single-day move because the market had priced itself for a surplus and had to reprice for a deficit within one delivery month.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary. The 14 June article is the next-day retrospective the brief's technique 1 describes: it names the cause of the rally that peaked on the 13th, and its event date sits inside the extended window. Probable, the source ceiling.

annotations.label: Heatwave gas-for-power demand and low wind
annotations.what_happened: The Cerberus heatwave peaked in the week to 24 July 2023 (47.8C at Syracuse on 24 July), lifting gas-for-power burn amid weak wind and keeping TTF above EUR40/MWh.
annotations.why_it_moved: Heat-driven cooling demand plus low wind raised gas-fired generation, tightening the prompt gas balance and lifting gas forwards.

annotations.label: Norwegian outages tighten supply into August
annotations.what_happened: European gas traded around EUR30/MWh at the start of August 2023 after falling 24% through July. Trading Economics reported that maintenance work and unplanned outages at Norwegian facilities had been supporting prices in the preceding weeks, Norway having replaced Russia as one of the largest sources of EU gas imports at roughly 25% of the total. The rebound had begun in late July: on 26 July the contract rose past EUR32 as renewed supply tightness met increased cooling demand, with planned Norwegian maintenance set to halt production the following month and fires near the Columbia Gas Transmission pipeline in the US cutting feed gas to LNG plants. Demand remained weak and storage was around 85% full.
annotations.why_it_moved: Gas Sep-23 is the final injection month, so it prices the last chance to top storage up before winter. Norwegian maintenance concentrated in exactly that month cuts the volume available for injection at the point where there is no time left to make it up, which is why the September contract could rise 8% on the week while the broader market was still 24% down on the month.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated one day before the trigger day and inside the window. Probable, the source ceiling.

annotations.label: Australian LNG strike threat
annotations.what_happened: The Australian LNG strike threat (Woodside North West Shelf; Chevron Gorgon/Wheatstone) persisted through mid-August 2023, keeping European gas elevated on fears of losing about 10% of global LNG supply.
annotations.why_it_moved: Continued risk to a large slice of global LNG kept a supply-competition premium in European gas forwards.

annotations.label: Australian LNG workers strike ultimatum
annotations.what_happened: In the week to 21 August 2023 Australian LNG workers issued a strike ultimatum, sending European gas soaring on renewed fears of disruption to about 10% of global LNG exports; power rose alongside gas.
annotations.why_it_moved: The hardened strike threat re-priced the risk of tighter global LNG, lifting gas and, via generation costs, power forwards.

annotations.label: Australian LNG strike fears recede (Woodside deal)
annotations.what_happened: Around 23-24 August 2023 Woodside reached an in-principle agreement with unions at its North West Shelf plant, easing fears of an imminent strike; benchmark European/UK gas fell roughly a third from the week's peak.
annotations.why_it_moved: Removing the near-term Woodside strike risk cut the LNG-disruption premium, sending gas forwards sharply lower.

annotations.label: Australian LNG strikes begin at Chevron plants
annotations.what_happened: The same episode as ref 43, caught by the later of two overlapping windows. European gas surged by as much as 11% to EUR36.2/MWh on Friday 8 September 2023 as union talks broke down and partial strikes began at Chevron's Gorgon and Wheatstone LNG facilities in Australia, which together supply more than 5% of the global market. Prices rose more than 6% again on Monday 11 September as the strikes continued and Norway's Troll field entered a third week of maintenance with greater capacity restrictions than first announced, and by 12 September the market was about 15% up on the month with unions signalling escalation and China reported to be seeking more than a dozen winter cargoes.
annotations.why_it_moved: The wider window captures the point at which the LNG squeeze fed through into power as well as gas: Electricity Oct-23 breached alongside Gas Oct-23 and Nov-23 because European power in October is still substantially gas-set at the margin, and a global LNG supply shock that raises the October gas price raises the October power price with it. The Chinese winter procurement reported on 12 September is what turned an Australian labour dispute into a competition for the same cargoes Europe needs.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated on the trigger day. Probable, the source ceiling. Same driver as ref 43; this row is recorded separately because it is a separate worklist ref with a wider window and a Both fuel scope.

annotations.label: Gassco widens Troll outage from 95 to 125 mcm
annotations.what_happened: European gas rose almost 7% on Tuesday 19 September 2023 after Norwegian gas system operator Gassco revised the details of a planned outage at the Troll field, expanding the affected capacity from 95 million cubic metres to 125 mcm. The revised outage was scheduled to run from 20 to 21 September. Trading Economics reported the market trading around EUR36/MWh on 20 September after that move, noting that ample European stockpiles and mild October weather forecasts were working the other way. The week ended more than 9% higher, with the Australian Chevron strikes resolved but Norwegian maintenance expected to persist into October and US LNG flows to Sabine Pass down 18% in a day.
annotations.why_it_moved: Troll is the single largest field supplying Europe and Gas Oct-23 was the front winter month, so a 30 mcm widening of an outage that lands right at the start of the heating season hits the contract with the least room to source a substitute. This is the primary-operator-data case the brief describes: the driver is a dated capacity revision published by the system operator, not a piece of sentiment.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary. Event date is Tuesday 19 September, the trigger day, taken from the article's reference to the previous session rather than its 20 September publication date - technique 1 in the brief. Probable, the source ceiling, though the underlying fact is a Gassco outage revision, which is primary operator data.

annotations.label: Australian LNG strikes end at Gorgon and Wheatstone
annotations.what_happened: On Friday 22 September 2023 the Offshore Alliance union settled with Chevron after mediation by Australia's labour regulator, ending two weeks of strike action at the Gorgon and Wheatstone LNG plants, which together account for over 5% of global LNG supply. The removal of the supply risk sent European gas lower, front-month TTF dropping 1.8% to about EUR 38.39/MWh and the UK equivalent falling 3.3%.

Settling the dispute removed that premium at a stroke. Because it was a global LNG supply story rather than anything European, it moved gas and the far power seasons together, matching the Both scope, and Electricity Win-28 fell 8.4% on the week.

annotations.label: Balticconnector rupture and Israeli field shut-in
annotations.what_happened: European gas soared on Monday 9 October 2023, up 15% to EUR43/MWh after a 5.6% jump the previous Friday. Two dated supply events landed over the weekend. Finland and Estonia observed an unusual pressure drop in the Balticconnector offshore gas pipeline on Sunday 8 October, shutting the link; the damage was later believed to be deliberate and repairs were expected to take months. Workers at Chevron's Australian LNG plants were also reported to be planning to resume strikes. Prices rose a further 12% on 10 October to approach EUR50, a six-month high.

Two simultaneous physical outages, one of them apparent sabotage of European infrastructure, reintroduced a security-of-supply premium that storage cannot substitute for: full tanks protect against cold, not against pipelines being cut. The Tamar shut-in compounds it by reducing Egyptian LNG exports, which are a European supply source.

annotations.label: Balticconnector pipeline damage (plus Israel-Hamas)
annotations.what_happened: On 8 October 2023 the Balticconnector gas pipeline between Finland and Estonia was damaged in a suspected deliberate act and shut, driving a roughly 15% Monday jump in European gas. Coinciding were the 7 Oct Hamas assault on Israel and Chevron's precautionary shutdown of Israel's Tamar field, adding a geopolitical-supply premium; TTF rose about 46% over the week to 12 Oct.
annotations.why_it_moved: A physical loss of European pipeline infrastructure plus Middle East supply/security fears revived the market's fragility premium, lifting gas and power forwards.

annotations.label: Israel-Hamas conflict lifts eastern-Med supply-risk premium
annotations.what_happened: Through mid-October 2023 European gas stayed elevated on the Israel-Hamas war: Israel had ordered Chevron to shut the Tamar offshore field and traders feared a wider conflict and disruption to eastern-Mediterranean gas/LNG, on top of the still-unresolved Balticconnector pipeline damage.
annotations.why_it_moved: Geopolitical escalation in a gas-producing region plus lost pipeline infrastructure kept a supply-risk premium in European gas forwards.

annotations.label: Strong Norwegian supply with EU storage effectively full
annotations.what_happened: Dutch and British gas prices fell on Tuesday 31 October 2023 as strong supply weighed on the market. Norwegian piped exports were nominated at 321 million cubic metres a day, up 11 mcm/d on the Monday, LSEG data showed, and European storage sites stood at 99.25% of capacity. Russian supply via Ukraine was stable at 42.4 mcm. The benchmark Dutch month-ahead contract fell 1.15 euros to 48.85 euros/MWh, the December contract slipped 0.60 euro to 51.70 euros/MWh, and the British November contract dropped 5.5 pence to 120 p/therm. LSEG analyst Saku Jussila also pointed to forecasts of slightly milder weather and rising northwest European LNG send-out from the start of November.
annotations.why_it_moved: Europe entered this winter with storage essentially full and Norway, its swing supplier, exporting at high rates. That combination removes the scarcity premium that had been priced into the deferred contracts since 2022: if the system can arrive at winter full and keep filling, the market no longer needs to bid up the following summer to secure refill volumes. That is why the breach sits in Sum-24 and Win-24 rather than at the prompt, and why power followed gas down.

annotations.label: Near-full storage outweighs a December cold snap
annotations.what_happened: European gas kept falling through the last week of November 2023, reaching about EUR44/MWh on Monday 27 November and EUR43 on 28 November, a seven-week low, before breaking below EUR40 on 29 November. Trading Economics attributed the decline to ample supplies more than offsetting forecasts of very cold weather across much of Europe in early December: storage in Germany and France was nearly full and Italy's reserves were above 96%, with EU storage at 97% and only slightly down from 98.4% the week before even as temperatures started to fall.
annotations.why_it_moved: This is the market deciding that a forecast cold snap was no longer a threat. Every contract that breached is a winter or summer 2024 delivery month, and each of them had been carrying some premium for the possibility that a cold December would drain European storage and leave the refill season starting from a hole. Storage at 97% going into December falsified that, so the premium came out of the whole strip at once - which is why Dec-23 through Mar-24 all fell within a point of each other. Power followed gas, giving the Both fuel scope.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated on the label date itself. Probable, the ceiling for that source.

annotations.label: Milder, windier weather cutting gas-for-power demand
annotations.what_happened: Dutch and British wholesale gas prices fell on Monday 11 December 2023 on expectations of higher temperatures and stronger wind generation, with steady LNG send-out and Norwegian pipeline flows holding at 347 million cubic metres a day. The Dutch January contract fell 2.53 euros to 36.10 euros/MWh, its lowest since 6 October, the February contract fell 2.45 euros to 36.60 euros/MWh, and the British day-ahead price dropped 4.10 pence to 91.00 p/therm. French nuclear availability was also expected to rise from about 45 GW to 51 GW by the Wednesday.
annotations.why_it_moved: Higher wind output displaces gas-fired generation directly, and milder temperatures cut heating demand, so the two together removed a large slice of December burn at a moment when supply was steady rather than constrained. Less gas burned in December means storage ends the winter higher and less has to be repurchased over the following injection season, which is why the breach lands in Gas Sum-24 at -11.1% rather than only at the front.

annotations.label: Mild winter outlook takes the gas curve to 3-month lows
annotations.what_happened: European gas fell below EUR34/MWh on 11 December 2023, the lowest in nearly three months, on muted demand and evidence of ample supply, with continental temperatures having returned to moderately above the seasonal norm after the cold snap at the start of the month. The UK benchmark did the same on 12 December, falling below 90 pence a therm to a three-month low on robust supply and expectations of a mild winter, with forecasts suggesting Northern Hemisphere winters would stay relatively mild through the start of January. EU carbon had fallen below EUR73 on 5 December, its lowest in over a year.
annotations.why_it_moved: Gas May-30 is six and a half years forward, so per the brief this is the curve moving with the market rather than anything to do with May 2030. What the market did in that window was mark the whole complex down as the winter risk that had supported it through the autumn failed to appear, and a thinly traded far-dated point followed the shift. A 4.2% move at that tenor is small in absolute terms and consistent with a general downward re-mark rather than a specific event.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary for both benchmarks, dated inside the window. Probable, the source ceiling. Deliberately not looking for a May 2030 story, per the brief's instruction on far-dated months. Note the contrast with ref 49, which shares this window: the gas curve fell and is attributable, while the single power point rose and is not.

annotations.label: Red Sea diversions delay Qatari LNG into Europe
annotations.what_happened: On Wednesday 24 January 2024 European gas rose to EUR29/MWh from a six-month low as Qatar faced delays shipping to Europe because of the conflict in the Red Sea. Ship-tracking data showed that since 15 January at least six shipments bound for Europe had taken the longer route around the Cape of Good Hope rather than transiting the Red Sea and Suez. The UK benchmark did the same, rising above 72 pence a therm on 25 January from a six-month low below 67, explicitly in line with the European move and driven by the same Qatari shipping delays. By 31 January the market was still being supported by the Red Sea reroutings, with production problems at Freeport added to the list.
annotations.why_it_moved: The contracts that breached are Feb-24 through May-24, the delivery months a diverted cargo actually misses. Routing around the Cape adds roughly two weeks to a Qatar-Europe voyage, so a diversion does not destroy supply, it moves it later in the curve and thins out the front. That is exactly the shape of the breach: the nearest months moved most, with the effect tapering as you go further out to May.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated on the label date itself. Probable, the source ceiling. Worth noting the rest of the week went the other way - the same archive has the market back near six-month lows on 25, 26 and 30 January - so this is a one-day spike on the Red Sea news rather than a sustained move, which matches a Trigger day move of +7.5% inside a wider weekly episode.

annotations.label: Record end-of-winter storage as heating season closes
annotations.what_happened: European gas fell through the end of March 2024 and into April. On 26 March it pulled back below EUR28/MWh as Norwegian supply surged into continental Europe, with the Vesterled pipeline redirecting flows, and as forecasts for the first week of April turned milder. By 3 April it had dropped below EUR26/MWh, a three-week low, on record gas storage levels as the winter season ended: EU storage stood at 58.72% of capacity at the end of March, three points above the previous year, leaving the bloc in a strong position to refill over the summer.
annotations.why_it_moved: Coming out of winter with storage at a record for the date removes the summer refill task that normally supports near-dated summer contracts, and Gas May-24 is the first full injection month. Power fell with it because European power in May is still substantially gas-set at the margin, which is what produces the Both fuel scope here: Gas May-24 down 8.3% and Electricity May-24 down 9.1%, the same event reaching both fuels through the same channel.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary. The 3 April article sits on the last day of the extended window and is the one that names the driver; the 26 March article is cited for where the decline started. Probable, the source ceiling.

annotations.label: Iran attacks Israel; escalation fears
annotations.what_happened: On 13 April 2024 Iran launched a large drone/missile attack on Israel, and Israel vowed to respond; European gas jumped, closing up 6.4% on 16 April in a fourth straight daily advance as traders re-priced Middle East supply risk.
annotations.why_it_moved: A direct Iran-Israel exchange raised the risk of disruption to regional gas/LNG and shipping routes, lifting European gas and power forwards.

annotations.label: Norwegian and UK outages tighten supply
annotations.what_happened: European gas rose above EUR29/MWh on Wednesday 24 April 2024, up from a two-week low, on disruptions to supply from Norway and Britain. Reduced flows of Norwegian gas to Britain and unplanned outages in the UK tightened the supply picture, with additional planned maintenance in Norway compounding it. This came after a fortnight in which the market had been driven by Middle East tensions - a three-month high near EUR34 on 16 April after the Iranian attack on Israel, then a fall back to EUR30 by 22 April as fears of an immediate Iranian retaliation receded.
annotations.why_it_moved: Gas Aug-29 is more than five years forward and has no exposure to a Norwegian maintenance schedule, so per the brief this is the curve following the market rather than the delivery month responding. The market rose that day on the outages, and a 3.5% move at that tenor is a modest re-mark in the same direction rather than a distinct event.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated one day before the trigger day and inside the window. Probable, the source ceiling. Not hunting for an August 2029 story, per the brief.

annotations.label: Mild ten-day forecast meets ample supply
annotations.what_happened: European gas fell towards EUR28/MWh on Monday 29 April 2024, the lowest in nearly three weeks, as forecasts of mild weather coincided with a backdrop of ample supply. New forecasts indicated moderately warm and mostly dry conditions across Europe over the following ten days, limiting demand for gas-intensive heating. The move was a 3.9% fall on the day, and it reversed the next session when LNG send-out into northwest Europe dropped from 2,096 GWh/d to 1,768 GWh/d and Norwegian flows fell on maintenance.
annotations.why_it_moved: Gas Mar-30 is nearly six years forward and carries no weather content, so this is the curve following the market. What matters for the record is that the market did move down on the trigger day and the dated reason is in the source; a 3.3% re-mark at that tenor against a 3.9% fall in the front is proportionate rather than anomalous.
annotations.notes: Trading Economics daily commentary, dated on the trigger day. Probable, the source ceiling. Not hunting for a March 2030 story, per the brief.

annotations.label: EU storage hits 90% two months before target
annotations.what_happened: European gas fell below EUR37/MWh on 21 August 2024, down from an early-month peak above EUR40, as European reserves approached full: storage hit 90% of capacity on 19 August, passing the EU's 1 November target more than two months early. The fall completed a reversal of the geopolitical spike earlier in the month, when prices had reached an eight-month high above EUR41 on 12 August on fears for Russian gas transiting Ukraine after the Ukrainian incursion around Sudzha.
